title: Planning a Presentation on Food Waste
context: Two students discuss a presentation with their tutor, who challenges their argument and their timing.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: Right — Tomas, Leyla, let's look at where you've got to with the food waste presentation. You sent me an outline. What's the argument?

script.speaker: Leyla
script.text: Before Tomas starts — we did rewrite the whole outline twice over the weekend, so apologies if it still reads a bit rough in places.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: That's exactly why we're doing this now rather than after you've printed it. What made you go back to it a second time?

script.speaker: Tomas
script.text: Honestly, the first version bored us, and if it bored us writing it, it was going to bore everyone else too.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: That is, without exception, the best reason there is to rewrite anything. Go on, then — where did you end up?

script.speaker: Tomas
script.text: We started with the household angle, because that's where most of the waste is. About seventy per cent of it in the UK happens after the food reaches someone's kitchen.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: That figure is right, and it's also the reason your first draft went wrong. If seventy per cent is domestic, what does that tell an audience they should do?

script.speaker: Leyla
script.text: Buy less. Plan meals. Which is what every campaign already says.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: And how well has that worked?

script.speaker: Leyla
script.text: Not very. That was our problem. We had four slides of advice nobody would follow.

script.speaker: Tomas
script.text: So we changed it. We're now arguing that the interesting waste isn't the largest share, it's the share that's easiest to move. And that's not households.

script.speaker: Leyla
script.text: Which sounds like a small thing to build a whole talk around, until you actually think about how the numbers work.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: Go on.

script.speaker: Tomas
script.text: Retail is only about two per cent of the total, which sounds trivial. But a supermarket makes a small number of decisions that determine what happens in millions of kitchens — how big the pack is, what the date label says, whether the offer is buy one get one free.

script.speaker: Leyla
script.text: It's a nice example, actually — even something as small as changing where the reduced-price stickers go on the shelf changes what a family throws away, multiplied across every store in the country.

script.speaker: Tomas
script.text: Exactly. Nobody notices one supermarket's decision. Everybody notices it once you add up every branch of every chain in the country.

script.speaker: Leyla
script.text: Which is really the whole pitch in one sentence, isn't it — small decision, huge multiplier.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: That's a much better argument. Where's your evidence for the date labels?

script.speaker: Leyla
script.text: There are trials where retailers removed 'best before' from fresh produce and measured what happened. The reductions were real but smaller than the press releases suggested. We want to be careful there.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: Good instinct. What's your source?

script.speaker: Leyla
script.text: A government-funded review from 2022. It pools about a dozen studies, so it's stronger than any single trial, but it does say the evidence quality is mostly moderate.

script.speaker: Tomas
script.text: Should we even mention the moderate-quality point, though? It feels like it undermines our own argument before we've made it.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: Say that out loud in the presentation. An audience trusts you more when you name the weakness than when they find it in the questions. Now — timing. How long have you got?

script.speaker: Tomas
script.text: Fifteen minutes, plus five for questions.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: And how many slides?

script.speaker: Tomas
script.text: Twenty-two at the moment.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: That's a slide every forty seconds. Cut it to twelve.

script.speaker: Leyla
script.text: Twelve? We'd lose the whole section on anaerobic digestion.

script.speaker: Tomas
script.text: I was going to say the same thing. It's the section we've both put the most work into so far.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: Which is the section I'd cut first. It's interesting, but it's about what to do with waste once it exists, and your argument is about preventing it. It belongs in a different talk.

script.speaker: Tomas
script.text: We could put it in the handout instead.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: Do that. What about the division of labour?

script.speaker: Leyla
script.text: I'm doing the evidence and Tomas is doing the retail case.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: Then swap the order. Open with the retail decisions, because that's the counterintuitive part and it earns you attention, and put the evidence review after it so it answers the doubt the opening creates. And whoever isn't speaking should be watching the clock, not the slides.

script.speaker: Leyla
script.text: That does make more sense — we were basically telling them the answer before asking the interesting question.

script.speaker: Tomas
script.text: I'll admit I only suggested the original order because I wanted to go second.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: Which is a perfectly human reason, and not a good one. Audiences forgive a shaky start far more easily than a flat ending, so open with your best material, always.

script.speaker: Tomas
script.text: Understood. When do you want the draft?

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: Rehearse it in front of each other first — properly, standing up, timed. Then send me the recording rather than the slides. I learn far more from three minutes of you talking than from twenty-two slides.

script.speaker: Tomas
script.text: Will do. Thanks for going through all of this with us.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: One more thing before you go. However this lands with the audience, the retail argument is the one worth defending hardest in questions, because it's the one people will instinctively push back on — everybody has a household habit they're proud of, and rather less of an opinion about supermarket policy.

script.speaker: Tomas
script.text: Good to know. We'll make sure we can back that part up properly, then.

script.speaker: Leyla
script.text: And I'll have the review's limitations ready in case anyone asks about the sample size.

script.speaker: Dr Okafor
script.text: That's the spirit. Send me that recording, and we'll find some time before the slot itself to run through it once more.

script.speaker: Leyla
script.text: Yes — genuinely useful, even the parts that stung a bit.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

questions.question: Why does Dr Okafor say the household figure led the students astray?
options: The figure they had used turned out to be quite inaccurate
It pointed them towards advice that campaigns already give
It applies only to countries outside the United Kingdom
questions.explanation: He confirms the figure is right, then asks what it tells an audience to do. Leyla answers “Buy less. Plan meals. Which is what every campaign already says.”

questions.question: What is the students' revised argument?
options: That the largest single source of waste deserves by far the most attention
That the share easiest to change matters more than the largest share
That households cannot reduce the waste they produce at all
questions.explanation: Tomas: “the interesting waste isn't the largest share, it's the share that's easiest to move. And that's not households.”

questions.question: Why does Tomas think retail matters despite its small share?
options: Supermarkets waste a great deal more food than they actually report
A few retail decisions shape what happens in millions of kitchens
Retail waste is now growing faster than household waste is
questions.explanation: “A supermarket makes a small number of decisions that determine what happens in millions of kitchens — how big the pack is, what the date label says…”

questions.question: What does Leyla say about the date-label trials?
options: The reductions were smaller than press releases suggested
No reductions of any kind at all were found in the published data
Only one retailer has ever tried the approach
questions.explanation: “The reductions were real but smaller than the press releases suggested. We want to be careful there.”

questions.question: What does Dr Okafor advise about the weakness in their evidence?
options: To leave it out of the presentation entirely
To state it themselves during the talk
To mention it only if somebody asks
questions.explanation: “Say that out loud in the presentation. An audience trusts you more when you name the weakness than when they find it in the questions.”

questions.question: Which TWO changes does Dr Okafor make to how Tomas and Leyla will present their argument?
options: Present the retail evidence before the review of the date-label trials
Whichever of them is not speaking should keep track of the time
Leyla should present the retail case and Tomas the evidence review
Rehearse sitting down, exactly as they will present to the audience
Send Dr Okafor the finished slide deck once it is ready
questions.explanation: Two changes are given directly. “Swap the order. Open with the retail decisions… and put the evidence review after it” supports the first option, and “whoever isn't speaking should be watching the clock, not the slides” supports the second. The division of labour itself does not change — Leyla keeps the evidence and Tomas keeps the retail case — so the third option reverses what actually changes. Dr Okafor asks them to rehearse “standing up”, not sitting down, so the fourth option contradicts the script. He also asks for “the recording rather than the slides”, so the fifth option is the opposite of what he requests.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS OR A NUMBER for each answer.

questions.sentence: Roughly ___ per cent of UK food waste happens after food reaches the kitchen.
questions.explanation: “About seventy per cent of it in the UK happens after the food reaches someone's kitchen.” Two per cent is the retail share.

questions.sentence: The talk lasts fifteen minutes with ___ minutes for questions.
questions.explanation: “Fifteen minutes, plus five for questions.” Fifteen is the talk itself, so the blank takes the question time.

questions.sentence: The tutor tells them to reduce the deck to ___ slides.
questions.explanation: “That's a slide every forty seconds. Cut it to twelve.” Twenty-two is the current number, not the target.
